planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it a sheltered spot out of harsh winter wind at the colder end of its range, since the evergreen foliage can be damaged by exposure in hard freezes.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath high, open tree canopy; Chinese leatherleaf mahonia is a tall, architectural evergreen shrub with long, upright canes topped by whorls of narrow, spiny-toothed, leathery leaflets, giving it a bold, almost tropical silhouette unlike the lower, mounding mahonias more commonly grown. In late fall into early winter it produces dramatic upright racemes of bright yellow, faintly fragrant flowers held above the foliage like candelabra, opening earlier than most other mahonias and providing valuable nectar for pollinators and hummingbirds during the coldest, leanest part of the year; blue-black, grape-like berries follow and are relished by birds. Its strongly vertical, sculptural habit makes it a striking accent for the back of a shaded border or a shady courtyard corner rather than a foundation planting. It is the parent, along with M. japonica, of the popular hybrid Mahonia x media selections such as 'Charity' and 'Winter Sun'. Prune out the oldest canes at ground level after flowering if the clump becomes leggy, to encourage fresh basal growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in very well-drained, deep sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; pygmy fringetree is adapted to the excessively drained sand of Florida scrub and does poorly in heavy or wet soil.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, deep sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; pygmy fringetree is a rare, federally listed endangered shrub endemic to the ancient sand ridges of central Florida, where it grows as a much smaller relative of the familiar white fringetree — a compact, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a small tree — producing the same delicate, fragrant, white, fringe-petaled flower clusters in spring on a fraction of the scale. Dark, olive-like fruit follows on female plants when a male is nearby for pollination. Because it evolved in the deep, fast-draining, nutrient-poor sands of Florida scrub, it needs sharp drainage and tolerates drought and poor soil far better than average garden conditions; wet feet or heavy clay are more likely to kill it than neglect. Grown occasionally by Florida native-plant specialty nurseries and used in native scrub restoration and low-water landscaping within its narrow natural range; site it in a lean, sandy, well-drained bed rather than a typical amended garden border.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Status Assessment

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to sandy, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Kalm's St. John's wort is extremely adaptable to soil moisture extremes, native to the rocky and sandy shorelines of the Great Lakes.

directions: Plant in average to sandy soil, tolerant of both seasonally wet and fairly dry conditions, in full sun to partial shade; Kalm's St. John's wort is a compact, rounded native shrub from Great Lakes shorelines and rocky lakeshores, valued for bright, sunny-yellow flowers with a prominent burst of long stamens that bloom over a long stretch of summer, set against fine-textured, blue-green foliage. Older stems develop attractive exfoliating, peeling bark that adds interest through winter after the leaves drop. It is remarkably adaptable to difficult sites — tolerating both periodic flooding and dry, sandy soil, as well as wind and some salt exposure — which makes it a useful, low-maintenance choice for rain gardens, pond and shoreline edges, and other spots with unpredictable moisture. Deadheading is not required for continued bloom; a light shearing in early spring keeps the mounded shape tidy and encourages fresh flowering wood. Pollinators, particularly bees, visit the flowers heavily.
